strengths: Combining Fourier neural operators, adversarially generated measures, and bootstrapped Sinkhorn targets is a useful contribution to amortized OT. The approach accommodates varying grid resolutions without requiring a target dataset or fully converged training labels.

The reported transfer results are substantial. Table 4 shows approximately 1.3–2.8% transport-cost error across dataset combinations, nearly matching MNIST-trained Meta OT on MNIST while substantially outperforming it elsewhere.

The experiments demonstrate large iteration reductions and measured speedups up to 7.4× over default initialization. Multiple costs, spherical experiments, resolution sweeps, and the appendix’s marginal-violation results strengthen the empirical evidence.

Quantitative barycenter results support the usefulness of the predicted potentials beyond scalar costs. Detailed architecture and training specifications, pseudocode, and a code/weights link help reproducibility.
weaknesses: The advertised universality guarantee does not apply to the implemented generator. Theorem 3 requires equal input/output dimensions and a Lipschitz bound below the skip coefficient; Appendix C instead uses 200 latent coordinates for two 64×64 outputs and explicitly does not enforce that bound. Consequently, the theorem cannot establish coverage for the actual training distribution. Proposition 5 provides a useful residual-error bound, but does not establish convergence of the alternating, stopped-gradient training procedure.

The mathematical conventions require substantive reconciliation. For the product-reference KL dual in Equation (3), the scaling vectors include marginal factors: u = μ·exp(f/ε) and v = ν·exp(g/ε). Proposition 1 omits these factors, so Proposition 2’s convergence result does not directly justify convergence of the learned ε log(v) without additional corrections. Equation (1) also has the wrong KL sign, and Algorithm 1 reports only the transport-cost term rather than the defined regularized objective. These inconsistencies obscure what the reported errors and downstream gradients approximate.

There are no controlled ablations isolating adversarial generation, bootstrapping, and the operator architecture. Comparisons against a fixed random generator and direct dual-objective training on the same synthetic measures would establish which components produce the gains. Comparing against Meta OT trained only on MNIST demonstrates useful transfer, but does not disentangle the proposed training method from differences in training-data coverage.

The efficiency evaluation does not fully support the state-of-the-art claim. Table 2 measures time to a ground-truth cost-error threshold unavailable during deployment; the appendix supplies marginal-violation curves but no corresponding timing comparison at practical stopping tolerances. Comparable wall-clock results for Gaussian and Meta OT initialization are missing, as are comparisons exploiting separable kernels for squared-Euclidean grid costs.

The geometry demonstrations contain additional methodological problems. Equation (11) omits the derivative of the outer Sinkhorn divergence’s source self-interaction term. Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to probability weights, which changes a nonuniform measure even when its gradient vanishes, so it is not the stated projected-gradient method. These formulas need correction and alignment with the implementation. Furthermore, superiority over GeONet is illustrated with one pair rather than aggregate quantitative errors. These issues weaken the broader geometry claims despite the promising barycenter results.
